item.title: Novel computational workflow for selecting virtual patient cohorts for in silico clinical trials
item.description: Objectives: In silico clinical trials are a well-accepted model-informed drug development (MIDD) tool to understand, optimize and predict the effect of drugs across diverse populations [1,2]. Generation and selection of virtual patients for simulating in silico trials remains an open area of research not least due to challenges of selecting virtual patients that are representative of the underlying physiological and clinical characteristics of individual subjects enrolled into clinical trials [3]. While virtual patients can be obtained by sampling sets of parameters from a calibrated non-linear mixed effects model, these may however generate biomarkers outside the expected range of observations, thus impacting the accuracy of in silico clinical trials predictions. To obtain a more representative virtual population, different algorithms can be applied to tailor plausible patient cohorts and yield calibrated virtual patients. In this work, we present a new virtual patient selection workflow using a minimal quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) model of chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. Methods: A QSP model of HBV disease progression incorporating the effect of standard-of-care therapies (peg-interferon and nucleos(t)ide analogues) was used to generate plausible patient cohorts corresponding to the Everest trial [4] (a real-world clinical study exploring how interferon therapy can achieve functional cure in chronically infected patients). To tailor plausible patients to a virtual cohort mimicking baseline characteristics of patients enrolled into the Everest project, we developed a computational algorithm based on a mixed-integer linear programming framework coupled to a multi-objective optimization genetic algorithm. Subsequently, the virtual patient cohort obtained with this algorithm was used to perform in silico clinical trials mirroring the Everest protocol to validate the workflow. Non-linear relationships between baseline characteristics, prognostic biomarkers, and dosing parameters with clinical endpoints were explored using in silico trials. Results: We show that: (1) the HBV QSP model captures longitudinal biomarker data from untreated patients as well as chronically infected subjects receiving standard-of-care therapies, (2) Plausible patients generated with the model capture HBV disease progression, (3) The novel computational workflow efficiently selects virtual patients matching HBsAg and viral load baseline Everest data distributions, (4) In silico trials that mirrored the Everest trial showed quantitative agreement with clinical end-points thus validating the workflow, (5) In silico trials were leveraged to identify and compare optimal dosing regimens and explore mechanistic pathways in responders and non-responders to interferon. Conclusions: This work proposes and validates a novel QSP-based computational workflow for performing in silico trials, generating mechanistic hypotheses, and identifying optimal dosing regimens.Citations: COI: DW, AN, AS, RD are employees of and hold shares in GSK. item.description: For modeling imprecise and indeterminate data for multi-objective decision making, two different methods: neutrosophic multi-objective linear/non-linear programming neutrosophic goal programming, which have been very recently proposed in the literatuire. In many economic problems, the well-known probabilities or fuzzy solutions procedures are not suitable because they cannot deal the situation when indeterminacy inherently involves in the problem. In this case we propose a new concept in optimization problem under uncertainty and indeterminacy. It is an extension of fuzzy and intuitionistic fuzzy optimization in which the degrees of indeterminacy and falsity (rejection) of objectives and constraints are simultaneously considered together with the degrees of truth membership (satisfaction/acceptance). The drawbacks of the existing neutrosophic optimization models have been presented and new framework of multi-objective optimization in neutrosophic environment has been proposed. The essence of the proposed approach is that it is capable of dealing with indeterminacy and falsity simultaneously.

item.title: A Hybrid Last-Mile Delivery System Using a Truck and Diverse Robotic Fleet
item.description: The integration of autonomous robots into last-mile delivery systems offers a promising solution to the limitations of conventional truck-based logistics. This study investigates a hybrid last-mile delivery system utilizing both homogeneous and heterogeneous robots, addressing scenarios in urban areas. To manage battery constraints for robots returning after rendezvousing with a truck, we propose mixed-integer linear programming models that incorporate battery recharging and swapping strategies. Our work explores optimal solutions for truck and robot routes and evaluates different robot combinations to minimize total delivery time. We also develop a three-phased heuristic algorithm to efficiently solve large-scale problems. The models are validated using case studies in Ulsan Metropolitan City, South Korea. It demonstrates that the battery-swapping strategy can reduce total delivery time by up to 50% compared to truck-only systems. The findings highlight the significance of extended robot driving ranges in urban areas to enhance delivery performance. A sensitivity analysis further examines the effects of factors such as customer node size, robot speed, number of robots, and robot ratios. This study addresses key gaps in the literature on hybrid truck-robot delivery systems and provides practical insights to enhance efficiency and reduce delivery times in urban areas.

item.title: A knowledge-driven nonconvex square-root regularization framework for joint group sparsity and structured smoothness
item.description: Structured sparse learning is a leading paradigm for high-dimensional data modeling, as it enables rigorous integration of domain-validated structural priors into the learning process. Among these priors, pre-defined grouped structure and piecewise smoothness are ubiquitous in real-world applications. However, most existing structured regularization methods are built on squared loss and convex penalties, rarely jointly model these two complementary structural priors, and suffer from two key limitations. Their optimal tuning parameters are sensitive to the unknown noise level $σ$ due to the squared loss. Meanwhile, convex penalties induce inherent estimation bias and severe over-shrinkage of large magnitudes. To address these issues, we propose a knowledge-driven Nonconvex Structured Smooth Adjustment for Square-Root Regularization (NS$^3$R), which unifies the $σ$-free square-root loss with a joint nonconvex $\ell_{2,q}$ penalty ($0 < q < 1$) to simultaneously encode group sparsity and structured smoothness priors. Theoretically, we establish rigorous non-asymptotic error bounds for the NS$^3$R estimator under a mild $(2,q)$-group restricted compatibility condition. Computationally, we develop an efficient double-screened IRLS with thresholding (DS-IRLS-th) algorithm, which adopts a nested double-screening strategy to reduce computational cost and improve numerical stability, with provable global convergence for the resulting nonconvex optimization problem. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that NS$^3$R consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in finite-sample settings.

item.title: On the stability of learning
item.description: Learning algorithms are usually analyzed under the assumption that informative gradients are continuously available. But this is not always true---learning signals in biological neural networks, for example, may be sparse, local, and only intermittently available at any given synapse. In this work, we show that if gradient information is noisy and only intermittently available, learning may be unstable. In particular, even if average learning dynamics converge to the correct optimum, variance in learning may be asymptotically infinite. We explore this point in a number of analytically tractable settings, including single-layer and multi-layer linear networks, and derive explicit conditions under which learning is stable. These conditions complement, but are conceptually distinct from, existing conditions related to the stability of stochastic gradient descent. Our work demonstrates that unbiased credit assignment is not enough for reliable learning; sufficiently frequent and informative feedback is also required, which yields an additional constraint on models of biologically plausible learning.

item.title: Optimal Graphon Control of Collective Dynamics
item.description: We study optimal control of non-linear graphon dynamics in which the interaction kernel itself is the control. Motivated by opinion formation in social networks, we ask how changing who influences whom can steer a population toward a desired outcome. We develop a framework using interaction kernels with bounded variation in the receiver label, providing compactness while accommodating finite networks. We prove existence of an optimal pair and show that finite-agent approximations recover the continuum optimal value under successive refinement of the network and initial data, with subsequential convergence of suitably chosen discrete optimizers. Numerical experiments use neural networks to approximate optimal controls for bounded-confidence and graphon Kuramoto dynamics, illustrating how changes in interactions can prevent fragmentation and promote synchronization.

item.title: A Globally Convergent Newton Method for Nonsmooth Optimization in the absence of Smooth Surrogates
item.description: We propose a globally convergent Newton method for convex composite optimization problems with polyhedral regularizers. The method rests on the observation that the proximal gradient step yields not only a new point but also a subgradient, which determines the face on which the linearization of the regularizer is exact. Minimizing a second-order model of the objective over this face produces a Newton direction that involves no generalized second-order information about the regularizer and is a descent direction for the objective itself. The method is therefore globalized by an Armijo line search on the original objective which, unlike forward-backward envelope techniques, requires only evaluations of the smooth component. We establish global convergence and local quadratic convergence to tilt-stable minimizers without any nondegeneracy condition, and show that the unit step is always accepted when the smooth component is quadratic, which yields a line-search-free method. The subproblems require only projections onto faces, which are explicit for the Lasso and nonnegative least squares and computable in linear time for the fused Lasso. Numerical experiments show that the method compares favorably with state-of-the-art solvers.

item.title: Strengthening AC optimal power flow relaxation through offline bound tightening and linear approximations
item.description: The alternating-current optimal power flow (ACOPF) problem is fundamental to power system operation and planning, but its nonconvexity makes globally optimal solutions of large-scale instances computationally challenging. Convex relaxations provide tractable lower bounds for assessing solution quality and supporting global optimization, although their effectiveness depends strongly on relaxation strength. This paper proposes an offline convexification and bound tightening framework for constructing strong linear programming (LP) relaxations for families of related ACOPF instances. Rather than repeating the tightening procedure for each instance, we compute variable bounds and second-order cone outer-approximation (SOC-OA) cuts offline using a demand-slack model and reuse them for subsequent instances with the same topology and admissible demand variations. Computational results on PGLib instances show that the fully offline approach achieves an average gap of $4.32\%$, compared with $3.80\%$ for the fully online approach, while achieving an average speedup of approximately $272\times$. The results demonstrate that offline convexification and bound tightening can recover most of the relaxation improvement of online tightening while significantly reducing the computational burden for repeated ACOPF evaluations.

item.title: On Exact Critical-Region Boundaries in Continuous-Time Multiparametric Optimal Control Problems
item.description: Continuous-time multiparametric model predictive control solves the optimal control problem once, offline, for every initial state, and divides the initial-state space into critical regions, each with its own control law and sequence of active constraints. A boundary between two regions is either a hyperplane, given by one linear equation, or curved. The curved boundaries have not been computed to date; a classifier has been trained instead to distinguish the regions, so the partition has been known only approximately. In this paper we show that a curved boundary can be computed exactly, without solving any optimal control problem. The method rests on one property. Once the sequence of active constraints is fixed, together with the instants inside it at which a constraint becomes active or inactive (the switching times) and the instant at which the change of the neighboring region first appears (the event time), every condition on a boundary is a linear equation in the initial state, so the computation of a boundary, curved or not, is exact. We fix one of these instants, a switching time or the event time, and solve the linear equations that correspond to it for the corresponding initial state on the boundary; stepping the fixed instant along the horizon yields the whole boundary. A hyperplane is the case in which no instant is left to fix. We illustrate the method on the Newell-Lee evaporator, which has seven critical regions and eight boundaries, four hyperplanes and four curved, computing one boundary of each type in full with the adjacent regions at its ends.

item.title: A Dynamic Inventory Rationing Model for Last-Mile Delivery of Medication in Liberia's Community Health Program
item.description: We study the dynamic allocation of scarce medications in Liberia's community health program. A central warehouse supplies a health facility and the Community Health Assistants (CHAs) it supervises. When a CHA runs out of medication, patients are referred to the facility, incurring travel costs if they complete the referral and remain untreated otherwise. Allocating inventory to CHAs allows more patients to receive treatment without traveling, while retaining inventory centrally preserves flexibility to respond to uncertain demand. The allocation problem must balance these considerations while accounting for fairness across locations. We formulate this problem as a finite-horizon stochastic control problem whose objective combines the costs of referrals and untreated patients with a demand-weighted fairness utility. Because standard dynamic programming methods are computationally intractable in this setting, we develop a continuous-time approximation that involves controlling the drift rate of a reflected Brownian motion. We then adapt the deep splitting method, using deep neural networks to approximate the value function and its gradient and compute a dynamic allocation policy. We calibrate the model using data on malaria cases among children in the Fangonda region of Lofa County, Liberia, and evaluate the proposed policy in the original discrete-time model. In the baseline setting, our policy reduces operating costs by about 6% relative to the strongest benchmark, the fairness-only policy, while retaining approximately 98% of its fairness utility. Additional experiments show that higher referral costs shift inventory toward CHAs and reduce local unmet demand, while greater demand variability increases our policy's performance over the fairness-only benchmark. Our model and computational approach provide a framework for studying similar last-mile allocation problems.

item.title: Continuous-Time Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Control: Limits, Duality, and Stability
item.description: A sampled robust control problem averages future values over disturbance laws, while its continuous-time counterpart evolves with an averaged drift. We establish a fluid limit connecting these two models for Wasserstein ambiguity sets. Under a uniform disturbance moment bound and subcritical growth, sampled Bellman values converge locally uniformly to the upper and lower values of a discounted differential game. The argument accommodates unbounded disturbances without requiring square-integrable increments. We also derive an explicit bound on the change in either game value when both the radius and center of the ambiguity set vary. For Euclidean disturbance space, uniform Lipschitz continuity in the disturbance, common state and cost Lipschitz bounds, and a discount rate exceeding the drift's state Lipschitz constant, this estimate converts distributional confidence bounds into uniform value approximation bounds. Static Wasserstein duality reformulates pointwise distributional optimization; affine disturbance dependence permits an exact reduction to a ball of means. Experiments illustrate the common limit and decreasing value error with sample size. For a nonlinear disturbance model, uniform shifts overestimate worst-case recovery speed by about 36\%. In a two-product inventory model, increasing ambiguity raises production near balance while reducing the region of full production in deeper backlogs.

item.title: Timed Recovery Safe Gradient Flows for Constrained Nonlinear Programming
item.description: This paper studies how to relax pointwise feasibility in continuous-time dynamics for inequality-constrained nonlinear programming while retaining a quantitative feasible-recovery guarantee. Existing safe gradient flows enforce forward invariance of the feasible set, which yields an anytime-feasible dynamics but can be overly restrictive for optimization because it suppresses transient infeasible motion that may be essential for effective descent. To address this limitation, we propose a timed recovery safe gradient flow that replaces pointwise feasibility with fixed-horizon feasible recovery. The proposed construction augments the state with a timer that records the elapsed infeasible duration and computes a minimum-norm correction to the nominal gradient flow through a pointwise convex quadratic program. We show that the resulting augmented safe set is forward invariant and that every trajectory initialized from the feasible set returns to it within every time window of length \(τ\). We further show that, in a strict interior inactive regime, the closed-loop dynamics reduces exactly to the nominal gradient flow and recovers the corresponding local convergence behavior. Numerical examples illustrate how the recovery horizon shapes the closed-loop behavior and corroborate the theoretical analysis.

item.title: A branch-and-filter method for mixed-integer linear programming
item.description: We develop a new tree-search framework for mixed-integer linear programming problems, which incorporates a filter mechanism as a node-acceptance device. The introduced branch-and-filter algorithm combines proper branching actions with a filter on integrality violation and an incumbent-dependent objective coordinate. Inspired by classical filter methods in nonconvex constrained optimization, the proposed method moves to a restoration phase whenever sufficient progress cannot be provided by the filter and funnel mechanisms, the latter of which is anchored at global relaxation lower bounds. Under mild assumptions, the introduced method either certifies infeasibility in finitely many iterations, or converges to global optimality. Moreover, we establish a total outer iteration complexity bound of order $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-1})$ to certification of an $\varepsilon$-optimal mixed-integer solution through fixed-integer linear programming recovery. We finally perform several numerical experiments to study the performance of branch-and-filter against benchmark solvers, under a branch-and-bound, a branch-and-cut, and a novel cell-deletion realization of the proposed restoration oracle.

item.title: Freeform Programmable Liquid Crystal Elastomers via Monolithic Integration of Co-Optimization and 4D-Printing
item.description: Liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs) are active materials capable of large, reversible thermally induced actuation, offering significant potential for applications such as artificial muscles and soft robotics. However, their broader deployment is hindered by the lack of a unified design-to-fabrication framework, the strong coupling among geometry, director fields, and manufacturing constraints, and the difficulty of reliably translating complex designs into physically realizable architectures. Here, we present an autonomous and monolithic integration of co-optimization and 4D printing that enables the end-to-end design-to-realization of versatile programmable LCE architectures with superior precision, complexity, and versatility. The proposed framework establishes a unified design strategy that co-optimizes the freeform multilayer geometry and fully continuous layer-specific director distributions, and subsequently translates the optimized fields into fabrication-ready DIW toolpaths through an automated manufacturing-aware pipeline. To bridge computation and realization, we develop an optimization-centered 4D printing approach with automated, fabrication-aware toolpath generation tailored for direct ink writing of LCEs. With the proposed design-to-fabrication paradigm, we experimentally realize architectures that exhibit complex, non-intuitive thermo-mechanical behaviors. Experiments achieve highly challenging prescribed functionalities beyond the reach of intuition-based approaches and show excellent agreement with numerical simulations across all samples. This work establishes a generalizable inverse design and physical realization of freeform programmable LCE systems, enabling function-oriented and optimization-driven intelligent LCE applications for next-generation soft robotic and responsive material engineering.

item.title: Distributed Attacker Assignment and Interception Control in Multi-Agent Target-Attacker-Defender Games
item.description: This paper addresses the Target-Attacker-Defender (TAD) game within a planar environment, focusing on the protection of a stationary target against incoming threats. To compensate for potential speed disadvantages of the defenders, we leverage geometric pre-positioning within an annular defense perimeter. The problem is formulated as an area interception problem, for which we propose a distributed multi-agent algorithm consisting of two primary modules: target allocation and interception control. For target allocation, an equitable region partitioning strategy is employed to divide the defense area into annular sectors and assign defenders to attackers. Under specified angular-separation and parameter conditions, the proposed partitioning mechanism ensures that each defender is assigned at most one attacker, thereby reducing the complexity of multi-agent assignment. For the control layer, movement protocols based on zero-sum differential games and coverage optimization are designed, achieving Nash equilibrium strategies while maintaining effective barrier coverage. Numerical simulations show that the proposed method enables slower defenders to intercept faster attackers through proactive deployment and maintains nearly constant local computation time as the swarm size increases.

item.title: Empirically Calibrated Differential Games for Simulating Driver Interactions
item.description: Game-theoretic models can resolve vehicle interactions without hand-written priority rules, but whether they describe human drivers once calibrated has rarely been tested. This study formulates a general-sum differential game of vehicle interactions at urban intersections, calibrates it to observed driving, and evaluates it on data not used for calibration. Each vehicle minimizes a cost that combines speed tracking, adherence to a map-derived lane route, control effort, gap keeping based on the intelligent driver model, a predictive conflict term, and a contact barrier, while perceiving the other vehicles with a delay. The game is solved with a feedback iterative linear-quadratic algorithm, and ten behavioral parameters per vehicle are calibrated by Bayesian optimization on trajectories recorded at four intersections in Washington, D.C. The calibrated game reproduces the trajectories of 819 vehicles with a mean position error of 1.00 m. When only each vehicle's route is known, as in a simulator, it is the most accurate of the compared models on 96 held-out vehicles (7.42 m), and ten-fold cross-validation shows that it is significantly more accurate than calibrated SUMO (by 3.61 m), an inverse reinforcement learning model (by 0.93 m), and independent and cooperative variants of the same model (by 0.33 and 0.32 m). The solutions, computed in 2.1 s for a typical interaction, are verified approximate equilibria. Finally, the conflict and steering weights, which the data do not identify, can be set from safety and comfort targets; together with a stiffer contact barrier, this removes the collisions that otherwise occur in 43% of tight closed-loop conflicts.

item.title: Regret-Based Max-Pressure Traffic Signal Control under Uncertain Traffic States
item.description: Max-pressure (MP) traffic signal control selects phases using pressure scores computed from estimated traffic states, but these states are uncertain and their consequences depend on whether they alter phase ranking and how much pressure is lost. This paper develops a decision-oriented Regret-Based Max-Pressure framework that represents uncertainty through phase-selection regret, defined as the pressure loss of a candidate phase relative to the pressure-maximizing phase under each plausible latent state. We propose Stochastic Regret MP, which minimizes expected regret under a calibrated residual distribution, and Distributionally Robust (DR) Regret MP, which minimizes worst-case expected regret over a Wasserstein ambiguity set. Robustifying regret rather than absolute pressure makes the formulation invariant to state-dependent pressure components shared by all candidate phases, thereby focusing robustness on relative phase quality. We further derive an explicit queue-linear pressure-loss bound and establish strong queue stability when the net-service reserve exceeds the resulting loss coefficient. Numerical experiments show that both methods reduce normalized true-state pressure regret by about 70% relative to Point-estimate MP, while DR Regret MP yields lower network queues than direct robustification of absolute pressure. In microscopic SUMO experiments on a 28-intersection real-world network, Stochastic Regret MP and DR Regret MP reduce mean delay by 18.9% and 14.9%, respectively, and retain benefits under detector undercount and failure. The results show that representing uncertainty through its decision consequences can improve reliable traffic control under imperfect state information.

item.title: Continuous-Time Mean-Variance Portfolio Selection Reinforcement Learning Problems for a Markov Regime-Switching System with No-Shorting Constraints
item.description: This paper is the first to study the continuous-time mean-variance portfolio selection problem with no-shorting constraints in a Markov regime-switching market using reinforcement learning (RL). The main challenge stems from the interaction between random regime shifts and portfolio non-negativity constraints, which typically causes the coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equations to lose smoothness across different state regions. Additionally, directly imposing no-shorting constraints on randomized policies disrupts their analytically tractable Gaussian structure, complicating both exploratory modeling and reinforcement learning. To address these challenges, we propose an auxiliary exploratory approach that limits the policy to a Gaussian distribution and applies the no-shorting constraint solely to its mean. We explicitly characterize the optimal policy for this auxiliary problem and demonstrate that, by appropriately selecting the exploration variance, its optimal mean policy exactly matches the optimal policy of the original constrained mean-variance problem. Building upon this analytical framework, we develop a model-free reinforcement learning algorithm that learns the optimal portfolio policy directly from trajectory data. Numerical experiments support the theoretical results and show that the proposed method can effectively recover the optimal no-shorting portfolio in a regime-switching market.

item.title: A stochastic mirror descent algorithm for mean-field control problems
item.description: We develop a stochastic mirror descent method for continuous-time McKean-Vlasov control with measure-valued controls and general Bregman regularisation. The dependence on the state law leads to a coupled Wasserstein-Bregman stability problem and to a McKean-Vlasov adjoint equation, which have no counterpart in classical stochastic control. We establish a first-order representation of the cost and prove its relative smoothness in two regimes: nonlinear dynamics with bounded cost derivatives, and affine state-law dynamics with linearly growing cost derivatives, the latter covering linear-quadratic (LQ) and more general nonquadratic models. Our regularity conditions in the control measure are formulated through directional finite increments and do not require second-order flat derivatives. We further introduce relative semiconvexity along admissible forward-backward trajectories, allowing compensation between the dynamics, running cost, and terminal cost beyond pointwise Hamiltonian convexity. This yields energy dissipation, an O(1/n) convergence rate at the convexity threshold, and geometric convergence when regularisation dominates relative nonconvexity. Explicit LQ criteria and numerical experiments illustrate the scope of the results.

item.title: Mapping Academic Sports Analytics: A Content Analysis of JQAS and JSA
item.description: Sports analytics has expanded rapidly in professional sports and mainstream culture, yet defining its academic core remains a challenge. In this paper, we provide an empirical map of the academic sports analytics landscape based on a systematic content analysis of approximately 700 papers published in two leading dedicated journals, the Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports (JQAS) and the Journal of Sports Analytics (JSA), between the years 2005 and 2024. We classify each paper by sport discipline, mathematical method, and core research area, identify recurring themes, and examine macro trends. We find game tactics, player evaluation, team ranking, result forecasting, and tournament design to be the most studied research areas in sports analytics. We highlight selected papers in each area, illustrating the wide range of mathematical methods used and sports disciplines analyzed. Our work offers a comprehensive overview of the questions, methods, and disciplines that characterize the field, serving as a foundational reference for practitioners and researchers in sports analytics.

item.title: A Robust Control Architecture for Multirate Systems and their Interconnections
item.description: We introduce a framework for analyzing and designing linear multirate control systems and their interconnections through the lens of robust control. The proposed approach models multirate systems as impulsive systems with multiple independent jump maps and corresponding jump-time sequences. We tackle analysis and design problems with stability, dissipativity, and robustness objectives, relying on a multi-clock-dependent Lyapunov function parameterization. Further, we develop a compositional approach for analyzing interconnections of multirate systems based on individual dissipativity properties. The theoretical conditions can be verified via linear matrix inequalities and they require weak assumptions on the sampling rates, allowing for asynchronous and time-varying sampling rates with or without separated time scales. The practicality of the framework is demonstrated with numerical examples.

item.title: MIACE and Monotone Tracking: Exact Tuning for First-Order Plants and Positive Cascades with Pure Delay
item.description: The Module of Integral Absolute Complex Error (MIACE) was created by me 23 years ago. It gave very nice behaviour to the transient response of the controlled systems I tested. It combines absolute tracking-error and equilibrium-centered command areas. For a stable unit-gain plant with known pure delay, an exact identity separates squared MIACE excess into a negative-area penalty and a weighted area imbalance. The resulting lower bound depends on the plant's first low-frequency moment and the delay. Every attaining response of a positive cascade is monotone, independently of controller structure. For a first-order plant, output variation and peak overshoot also admit quantitative bounds. Exact conditions identify the unique positive PI controller attaining the delayed bound; filtered PID extends attainment beyond this PI range. For cascades of arbitrary order, Hermite interpolation and a finite-support delay remainder construct proper rational controllers of the same order, with internal exponential stability proved by positive convolution representations. An exponential-moment characterization then closes the attainment question when internal delay blocks are allowed: an ordinary command attains the bound if and only if $α>μ+δ-1$. An explicit internal-model controller realizes every feasible weight and delay. A sharp amplitude-cap condition determines the least command peak among all attaining responses and the complete capped sign-preserving area front. A small-gain estimate supplies an explicit MIACE deviation bound under delay error. A storage balance also extends the exact MIACE identity and monotone attainment to a nonlinear first-order class without delay. Independent physical integrations retain delays exactly; quadratic comparisons provide complementary benchmarks.

item.title: On the Limits of Stochastic Push-Pull over Time-Varying Digraphs
item.description: Stochastic Push-Pull achieves linear speedup with respect to the network size $n$ on static strongly connected digraphs, but whether this speedup persists on time-varying networks remains unclear. In this work, we construct a quadratic decentralized problem on period-two networks showing that stochastic Push-Pull may fail to attain linear speedup over time-varying digraphs. For $p$-periodic networks, we identify an effective node count $n_{\mathrm{eff}}\le n$ that governs the leading stochastic term. Specifically, for smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish convergence upper bounds and matching lower bounds for stochastic Push-Pull with constant stepsizes, both exhibiting the leading-order dependence $Θ(1/\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{eff}} T})$. When $p=1$, the identity $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=n$ recovers the usual linear speedup for static digraphs. However, periodic networks can have $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=o(n)$, demonstrating the loss of linear speedup under temporal variation. Numerical experiments illustrate effective-count scaling and the separation between static and periodic networks, consistent with our theoretical findings.

item.title: On the closure under barycenters of location-scatter families with a normalized generator
item.description: We provide an example of a normalized absolutely continuous probability whose location-scatter family (LSF) does not contain all the 2-Wassertein geodesics passing through its elements. In particular, we find a counterexample for Corollary 4.5 in [2]. Finally, we prove that LSFs with a (possibly singular) radially symmetric generator are closed under 2-Wasserstein barycenters.

item.title: Sharpness-aware Orthogonalized Momentum Algorithms
item.description: Adversarial sharpness penalty per iteration of a base optimizer, known as sharpness-aware minimization (SAM), is an accepted technique to improve generalization in deep learning. Recently, Muon has emerged as a dominant optimization algorithm for training large language models (LLMs). It achieves lower sample complexity for heavy-tailed gradient updates - a phenomenon common in LLM training. However, sharpness penalties with Muon updates are yet largely unexplored in the literature. Moreover, the behavior of SAM under heavy-tailed noise is unknown both theoretically and empirically. A potential reason for this gap is the additional cost of extra gradient computation per iteration for penalty perturbations in SAM, which becomes prohibitive for LLMs. This paper introduces Sharpness-aware Orthogonalized Momentum Algorithm (SOMA) to combine a computationally efficient and theoretically grounded perturbation scheme with the Muon algorithm. The key idea is to use stale (purely) stochastic gradient noise for adversarial perturbations. Theoretically, we show that SOMA's sample complexity is invariant to the perturbation direction. We provide explorations and insights into SOMA's robustness to heavy-tailed gradient noise. We extensively explore SOMA's efficacy in (a) mitigating quality degradation due to post-training quantization, and (b) catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning of LLMs.

item.title: L0-Norm-Based CycleGAN for Unpaired Brain CT-to-MR Synthesis
item.description: Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance (MR) imaging provide complementary information for the brain, but acquiring both modalities is not always possible. The cycle-consistent adversarial network (CycleGAN) enables unpaired CT-to-MR synthesis, but because the standard L1-norm cycle?consistency penalty grows linearly with the residual magnitude, the network tends to focus on large residuals. This paper introduces an L0-norm-based cycle?consistency term, in which the L0-norm is approximated by a smooth and bounded function. This approximation not only increases sensitivity to small residuals but also effectively suppresses the influence of large residuals. The proposed model and an otherwise identical L1-norm baseline were trained on 102 images and evaluated on 9 test images. The proposed model achieves a lower mean squared error (0.02746 versus 0.03464, a 20.7% reduction), a higher mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (15.80 versus 14.77 dB), and a higher mean structural similarity index (0.5689 versus 0.5407). It also has a lower maximum MSE and higher minimum PSNR and SSIM than the baseline. These results indicate that modifying the cycle-consistency penalty can improve reconstruction accuracy on this dataset.

item.title: Dual companions and improved regularity of Lagrange multipliers in optimal control
item.description: We investigate optimal control problems whose state equation takes the form $\mathcal{A}x-\mathcal{B}u=b$, where $\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{P}'$ is an isomorphism from a Banach state space $\mathcal{X}$ onto the dual of a reflexive Banach space $\mathcal{P}$. The adjoint equation involves the Banach space adjoint $\mathcal{A}':\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{X}'$, so that, in general, state and multiplier are of different regularity. For particular classes of partial differential equations, the typically weaker regularity of the multiplier is improved a posteriori by bootstrapping. In this work, we provide an abstract foundation for this methodology on the operator level. More precisely, we show that whenever the state cost extends to a differentiable function on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ in which $\mathcal{X}$ is densely embedded, as for $L^2$-tracking costs on Sobolev-type state spaces, the multiplier automatically lies in a subspace of $\mathcal{P}$, the dual companion, on which $\mathcal{A}'$ restricts to an isomorphism onto $\mathcal{H}'$. This yields an optimality system with balanced regularity, where state and multiplier solve equations of the same type. In applications, the dual companion can be identified by integration by parts in time or space. We illustrate the framework by linear elliptic and parabolic equations, Cauchy problems governed by general $C_0$-semigroups, and a wave equation with accumulated-state observation.

item.title: Who pays for urban environment management? The role of the third-party service provider
item.description: The dominant contemporary paradigm of direct state-led urban environmental regulation entails significant risks, including high administrative burden, frequent conflicts with polluting entities, and economic vulnerabilities for those sources. To address these deficiencies, this paper integrates third-party service provider (TPSP) into China's existing management framework as a beneficial extension beyond conventional government intervention. Utilizing an evolutionary game approach, we compare two distinct institutional settings, a non-integration management mode and an integration management mode, and scrutinize the evolutionary dynamics across both two- and three-dimensional systems. To enhance system robustness, we embed a strategic behavior-based dynamic punishment mechanism that effectively eliminates the perturbing effects of varied penalty rules, thereby steering all stakeholders toward an ideal stable state. This comparative institutional analysis isolates the marginal contribution of third-party intermediation, specifies when outsourcing environmental services outperforms direct government enforcement, and reframes evolutionary game theory as a design device for institutional self-correction. Furthermore, a predefined variable importance analysis is conducted to highlight critical factors warranting attention in practical policy implementation. Extensive simulation experiments, carried out under diverse system-level and parameter-level conditions, validate the theoretical properties of our model. The findings offer concrete managerial insights to inform the formulation of more effective urban environmental supervision regulations.

item.title: Contextual Decision Making: Predictive or Generative
item.description: Contextual decision making uses observed covariates to guide decisions under uncertainty. Two natural approaches are predict-then-optimize (PtO), which learns the conditional expected objective, and generate-then-optimize (GtO), which learns conditional uncertainty and optimizes using generated scenarios. We study when each approach is preferable by examining how the choice of learning target affects statistical accuracy and optimization tractability. Although PtO learns a narrower target, our regret bounds show how differences in smoothness can offset GtO's additional dimensional burden. Exploiting smoothness also raises an optimization tradeoff: within the class of nonnegative-weight PtO methods studied, a lower bound limits the gains from additional smoothness, while more flexible methods may introduce signed weights and lose the guarantee of preserving convexity. GtO preserves scenario-wise convexity, but requires learning a richer object and generating scenarios for optimization. Synthetic experiments and a real case study illustrate how these tradeoffs vary with data availability and problem structure. Together with the scope for reusing a model across tasks, our findings provide practical guidance for choosing between the approaches without identifying a universal winner.

item.title: A Stationary Mean-Field Model for Carbon Market Stability Reserve
item.description: We formulate the design of a market stability reserve as a stationary mean-field singular control problem. The allowance balance follows a regime-switching diffusion, while the regulator injects or withdraws allowances through bounded-variation controls. The objective trades off the average allowance balance, its stationary dispersion, deviations from a long-run target, and intervention costs. The optimal policy is a regime-dependent band rule characterized by four reflecting thresholds. Its computation reduces to a scalar fixed-point problem combining a coupled variational inequality with the invariant distribution of the reflected process. A calibration to the EU ETS yields thresholds of the same order of magnitude as the existing Market Stability Reserve rule. Comparative statics show that volatility is the main determinant of the intervention band, whereas the frequency and duration of crisis regimes have limited effects. A simpler two-threshold policy based on average regime dynamics closely reproduces the optimal regime-dependent policy in terms of liquidity and intervention volumes.

item.title: Regret-Based Scenario-Tree Construction for Multistage Stochastic Programs with Deterministic Constraints
item.description: Scenario trees are widely used to discretize multistage stochastic programs into forms that are tractable for numerical optimization. Yet, traditional scenario-tree construction methods are typically based on statistical similarity between the original uncertainty process and its discretization, and may fail to preserve the aspects of the uncertainty that matter most for decision-making. This paper shows that, under a fixed probability measure and deterministic feasibility constraints, the gap between the optimal value of the original multistage stochastic program and that of its scenario-tree approximation decomposes exactly into a sum of nodewise regret terms, each measuring the optimality loss at a particular node. This decomposition provides a clear target for scenario-tree construction: minimizing total regret across the tree. Motivated by this result, we propose a practical two-phase construction method for repeated stochastic optimization. In an offline phase, computationally inexpensive surrogates for decision regret are learned from data, and in the online phase, these surrogates guide scenario-tree construction. The resulting framework retains the structured optimization and constraint-handling capabilities of multistage stochastic programming while exploiting learned information about the uncertainty to make more effective use of a limited scenario-tree budget. Numerical experiments on multistage stochastic storage and production-planning problems show that, for a fixed tree size, the proposed method constructs higher-quality scenario trees and achieves better closed-loop performance than traditional scenario-tree construction methods.

item.title: Necessary and Sufficient Criteria for Global PID Regulation of Nonlinear Uncertain System
item.description: Although classical PID control is widely used in engineering practice, identifying all PID gains that guarantee global regulation of nonlinear uncertain dynamics remains challenging. For a class of second-order nonaffine systems under one-sided derivative bounds, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for global PID regulation: a fixed PID controller globally regulates the entire infinite-dimensional uncertainty class if and only if it regulates a single boundary linear system. Applying the Routh--Hurwitz criterion to this boundary linear system yields the exact admissible PID gain region. To establish this equivalence, we prove a structured Markus--Yamabe theorem for third-order integrator chains under uniform derivative-ratio conditions. Its proof combines a two-dimensional storage function constructed via viscosity solutions of a Hamilton--Jacobi equation with a scalar comparison argument. We further show that the same PID gain region remains exact for multidimensional affine systems under symmetry assumptions on the state partial Jacobians and the input matrix.

item.title: Superlinear Convergence of Cyclic Gradient Methods with Historical Ritz Step Sizes
item.description: Simplified spectral models predict dimension-dependent superlinear convergence for gradient methods, but the corresponding behavior of actual iterations remains only partially understood. Historical methods introduce an additional difficulty: the gradients defining the step sizes differ from those receiving them. We study this offset for cyclic reuse of historical Ritz step sizes on strictly convex quadratics. Within the existing limited memory steepest descent with retards (LMSDR) family, a rolling cyclic Ritz (RCR) rule reuses $m$ historical Ritz values $\ell$ times per cycle, ending with a complete sweep. At $q=m+1$ active distinct eigenvalues, an exact delayed recurrence gives almost-everywhere doubly exponential convergence with an explicit rate and exceptional weights. Nonempty open basins also exist for $m+1<q\le2m$ and $\ell\ge4$. Rebuilding the history from each cycle-start gradient costs $m$ additional updates and gives sampled cyclic Ritz reuse (SCR) a cycle-end map determined by the current weights. Under uniform sampling bounds, SCR converges doubly exponentially almost everywhere when $(2\ell-1)^m>\binom{q-1}{m}$. Increasing $\ell$ admits larger $q$ for fixed $m$. The guarantee extends to history-dependent choices from finite sampling menus under a bound on the number of admissible sampling sequences. Geometrically spaced decisions retain the SCR condition and rate range. Every update is counted, including sampling; a numerical illustration compares finite-tolerance update counts.

item.title: A Proximal Gradient Method for Nonconvex Nonsmooth Optimization with Applications
item.description: We study a proximal-gradient method for the sum of a convex smooth function $g$ and a possibly nonconvex, nonsmooth, strongly quasar-convex regularizer. The gradient step is weighted by the quasar-convexity parameter, so, for step sizes in the descent range, the iteration decreases a weighted objective, while the unweighted sum serves for comparison. We establish a geometric envelope around every global minimizer of the unweighted objective, with an explicit radius independent of the step size; a common minimizer yields global linear convergence. We also prove that every critical point $u$ of the weighted objective lies within an explicit multiple of $\|\nabla g(u)\|$ from every global minimizer of the unweighted objective. Together with an optimized composite comparison, this yields asymptotic distance bounds. An example shows that the two objectives can have different critical points. For power-regularized least squares with powers between zero and one, descent provides a confinement ball for the sharp local modulus, and support identification combined with a KL argument yields whole-sequence convergence.

item.title: G-ORACLE: A Fast Geometric Method To Explore All Near-Optimal Designs for Energy Systems
item.description: Modeling to Generate Alternatives (MGA) methods explore the near-optimal solutions of energy system optimization models (ESOMs), i.e., alternative planning pathways whose cost lies within a small predefined slack of the optimum but which can differ substantially in technology composition, regional distribution, and environmental impacts. Among MGA methods, ORACLE uniquely guarantees convergence to the near-optimal set within a targeted tolerance by iteratively refining inner and outer polytope approximations. At each iteration, given a trial point, it solves a problem as hard as the ESOM to find the nearest near-optimal solution to it. However, the trial point is obtained by solving a bilevel problem whose solution time grows rapidly with the number of iterations and eventually dominates the computational cost of the method. To eliminate this bottleneck, we present G-ORACLE, which exploits the fact that an optimal solution of the bilevel problem is always attained at a vertex of the outer approximation. G-ORACLE therefore replaces the bilevel problem with incremental vertex enumeration by the double description method and one convex projection per vertex, while retaining the convergence guarantee of ORACLE. A supporting-hyperplane check further avoids unnecessary recomputation of these projections as the inner approximation grows. We evaluate G-ORACLE on an electricity-only PyPSA-Eur model, exploring the near-optimal space of the installed capacities of six generation and two storage technologies. While ORACLE's bilevel problem exceeds 20 minutes at iteration 64, G-ORACLE performs the trial-point search in at most 14 seconds throughout 240 iterations, leaving the ESOM solves as the only significant computational cost.

item.title: Multiplicative vs. Additive State Coupling in Learned Optimizer Schedules
item.description: We learn schedules for a continuous penalty relaxation of MAX-CUT by backpropagating through an unrolled classical solver. A state-blind schedule generalizes to instances substantially larger than those used for training. A state-adaptive bilinear schedule also generalizes out of distribution, outperforming its untrained baseline across 15 seeds ($t=4.1$). By contrast, an additive ablation with identical inputs and output heads is statistically indistinguishable from the bilinear model in distribution but performs worse than its own baseline out of distribution ($t=-11.7$). This separation appears without regularization and persists across a $30$ round weight-decay sweep: the bilinear advantage remains significant at every tested value, whereas the additive model never recovers. The results in this setting isolate how solver state enters the schedule, rather than state adaptivity alone, as the architectural distinction associated with out-of-distribution transfer.

item.title: Non-singlets and the phase diagram of Matrix Quantum Mechanics
item.description: The quantum mechanics of one $N\times N$ Hermitian matrix in the infinite $N$ limit is well known to define a two-dimensional string theory when the quartic coupling constant $g$ is tuned to a special negative value $g_*$. We study the thermodynamics of this Matrix Quantum Mechanics (MQM), treating the SU$(N)$ symmetry as a global symmetry. Crucially, the non-singlets, i.e. states in non-trivial representations of SU$(N)$, implement the effects of vortices on the discretized worldsheets. This random lattice model has the low-temperature $c=1$ and high-temperature $c=0$ phases, with the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition separating them. We map out the phase diagram in the coupling--temperature plane, which is separated by the critical stability curve $T_c(g)$ extending from $g_*< g <0$. We study this curve using the non-perturbative matrix bootstrap and low- and high-temperature perturbation theory, which explain the thermal instability. At low temperatures, thermally excited non-singlets backreact on the Fermi sea of matrix eigenvalues, causing it to spill over. At high temperatures, the theory is described by an effective matrix integral obtained by dimensional reduction on the thermal circle; the eigenvalue distribution of the zero mode becomes unstable at the critical coupling. We conjecture that the BKT transition occurs at a special point on the critical curve and estimate its position. Finally, we switch to the regular square lattice and study the MQM-inspired Villain model, where the link factor is the one-dimensional propagator on a circle. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we map out the BKT transition in this model.

item.title: Subgraph Isomorphism, Integer Linear Programming, and Lattices: A Linear Algebraic Framework
item.description: The subgraph isomorphism problem (SGI) asks a deceptively simple question: is a graph B found inside a parent graph A? Famously NP-complete and the subject of volumes of study, attempts to practically solve subgraph problems typically require specialized software or the focused application of problem-specific theoretical knowledge. Here we present a straightforward linear framework that neatly joins SGI to lattice theory and constrained satisfiability and, importantly, yields an easily implemented algorithm that naturally leverages consumer-grade hardware and off-the-shelf libraries to compete with state-of-the-art specialized solvers. We additionally show practical realizations in approachable settings, along with some benchmarks that reduce 6+ hour computations to seconds. Aimed at readability, we develop a series of computable algebraic invariants and demonstrate their application to familiar problems such as the Knight's Tour, with a focus on providing an accessible entry point for researchers in graph theory, abstract algebra, and students in general.

item.title: Blind Random Search with Noisy Measurements: Almost Sure Convergence and Convergence Rates
item.description: Blind random search is a simple global optimization method that only requires the value of the loss function, without needing gradient information or an explicit loss model. However, its classical formulation assumes that the loss evaluation is noise-free, which limits its direct application to practical problems with noisy measurements. We extend blind random search by combining a vanishing acceptance threshold with the running average of noisy loss measurements. Under the stated assumptions, we prove that the proposed algorithm converges almost surely to the global minimizer. We further analyze the rate at which the loss at the current estimate approaches the minimum loss. For low-dimensional cases, we obtain an almost sure asymptotic upper bound on the difference between the two, and for high-dimensional cases, we prove that this difference, suitably scaled, has an exact Weibull limiting distribution.

item.title: Concurrent Space-Based Observer Placement and Scheduling for Cislunar Space Domain Awareness
item.description: As interest in cislunar space grows, so does the need for space domain awareness (SDA) capabilities to safely support missions. To enhance cislunar SDA capabilities, the use of space-based observers has been proposed. Prior research has explored optimizing observer placement but has not considered scheduling limitations. We propose a mixed-integer linear programming formulation that concurrently optimizes the placement and scheduling of space-based observers for cislunar SDA. Our work considers three aspects of observer scheduling: sensor tasking, communication, and charging. We utilize a scenario-based approach that generalizes observer placement for unknown targets while applying scheduling constraints to each scenario. However, this problem quickly becomes difficult for commercial solvers to handle as the number of scenarios grows. As an alternative, a column generation approach is employed to introduce well-performing schedules into the problem for each orbital slot. A comparative analysis is performed across multiple instances to evaluate the performance of column generation against that of a commercial solver. A case study is then conducted in which the performance of the observers' placement from the concurrent formulation is tested against a set of validation target sets and compared with the performance of two baselines in which placement and scheduling are performed sequentially.

item.title: Statistical inference for boundary constrained parameters
item.description: Estimation and inference under boundary constraints arises in many areas of statistics, but the available asymptotic theory remains limited and fragmented relative to the classical case, where the parameter lies in the interior of the parameter space. In this paper we derive a boundary-constrained analogue of the standard asymptotic expansion for a minimiser of a loss function, in which the deviation of the estimator from the population parameter is decomposed over lower-dimensional subspaces determined by the directional derivatives at the minimiser. Using this decomposition we show that the limiting distribution of the estimator is a mixture of point masses and truncated skew-normal distributions, with mixture probabilities determined by the directional derivative conditions. A consequence of this result is that the constrained and unconstrained coordinates do not separate: the presence of parameters on or near the boundary affects the sampling distribution of the unconstrained parameter estimators. We apply the expansion to obtain the asymptotic distribution of the quasi log-likelihood ratio statistic under a range of null hypotheses, and since the resulting mixture is not pivotal in the quasi-likelihood setting, we propose a simulation-based procedure for approximating critical values. The framework unifies and simplifies several existing results. We illustrate the methodology by testing for interactions in exponential family graphical models, where the parameters are subject to compatibility constraints that ensure a joint distribution exists.

item.title: First-order Methods for Variational Inequality Problems with Semi-Infinite Constraints
item.description: This paper studies first-order methods for monotone variational inequalities with semi-infinite constraints and presents this model as a framework covering constrained saddle-point problems, robust optimization, distributionally robust function-constrained optimization, and generalized Nash equilibrium formulations. Since feasibility must hold over infinitely many indexed constraints, direct projection onto the full feasible region is generally difficult. Therefore, we propose a single-loop primal-dual constraint extrapolation method (PD-ConEx) that updates primal variables, Lagrange multipliers, and worst-case constraint indices using first-order information, linearization, extrapolation, and projections only onto simple sets. We establish convergence guarantees for smooth and nonsmooth regimes, showing how the achievable rates depend on strong monotonicity and strong concavity of the index block. For coupled convex-concave saddle-point problems, strong convexity in the minimization block can accelerate its smooth terms even without strong concavity in the maximization block. We also develop an adaptive smooth variant with $O(1/K)$ VI-gap and feasibility guarantees without an a priori bound on generated multipliers. Moment-based and Wasserstein distributionally robust models fit within the framework, and numerical experiments on robust quadratic instances and distributionally robust learning illustrate the method's optimality and feasibility behavior.

item.title: Joint Service Depth and Priority Design in Queueing Systems
item.description: In AI-assisted service systems, the server can choose how much processing effort to spend on each job, which we call the service depth. Deeper reasoning improves output quality but occupies the server longer and increases congestion, and the realized processing time remains random because AI models are probabilistic and tasks vary in complexity. We study the joint design of service depth and priority in a single-server queue whose customers differ in delay sensitivity, with the goal of maximizing social welfare. For each customer type, the decision maker chooses a priority level and a service depth, and service times are exponential with mean equal to the chosen depth. With two customer types and linear service values, we characterize the centralized optimum. Counterintuitively, it prioritizes the patient type and gives it a smaller service depth when patient customers are sufficiently prevalent. When delay sensitivity is private, however, incentive compatibility requires the impatient type to receive a weakly shorter sojourn time, so the optimal price menu never prioritizes the patient type. Consequently, there can be a welfare gap between the centralized decision maker's optimal control policy and the optimal decentralized pricing mechanism. With a continuum of types, the centralized optimum is monotone: more delay-sensitive customers receive weakly smaller depth and higher priority, so the optimum can be implemented by a price menu with no welfare loss. Allowing randomized depths similarly closes the gap in the two-type model. Finally, we calibrate an agentic AI service system using published coding-agent trials from DeepSWE and numerically examine priority inversion, the value of joint design, and the welfare gain from personalization.

item.title: When Are Nesterov Trajectories Eventually Locally Minimizing?
item.description: We revisit the variational characterization of Nesterov's celebrated method and study when Nesterov trajectories are eventually locally minimizing in a variational sense, a notion that we define precisely. We show that this question is equivalent to the nonnegativity of an associated Schrödinger operator acting on variations of the trajectory. For power objectives of the form \[ f(x)=\frac{1}{p}\|x\|^p \] (where $\| \cdot\|$ denotes the Euclidean norm), we give a complete characterization: Among all exponents $p\ge 2$, the Nesterov trajectory with non-zero initial position is eventually locally minimizing if and only if $p=4$. We further interpret this exceptional exponent through the stability theory of semilinear elliptic equations.

item.title: Protect the Decision, Not the Disaster: Regret-Robust Capacity Sizing and Positioning with Transportation Recourse
item.description: An operator who positions mobile resources before a disruption faces two uncertainties that are usually treated as one: how the joint state of demand and travel conditions will vary, and which part of the resulting cost the positioning decision can actually change. Standard distributionally robust optimization (DRO) protects total cost, and therefore spends much of its protection on disruption costs that every feasible design would pay. This paper evaluates the worst-case regret of a design and compares it with the worst-case premium of total-cost DRO, and shows that the regret-to-premium ratio can be bounded before any robust model is solved: from marginals for the dependence question, and from single-scenario optima and one transport linear program for the regret question. The worst-case law is a relabelling of the operating record, reassigning every recorded period wholesale to another recorded period, except at most one, which is split. The comparator that exposes the largest worst-case regret is found by a single mixed-integer program. We derive an explicit radius where the sample-average design is exactly regret-robust. For finite scenario and design sets we compute a design's worst-case regret exactly, bound it from quantities a planner already has, and show on fleet and EMS data how law-relative regret changes capacity and positioning choices relative to sample-average and worst-cost planning. We apply the decision tree to several years of New York fleet data, including the year before Hurricane Sandy, and to two emergency-service events. The test flags the pre-Sandy year as exposed. The training-support regret bounds cover realized test regret in three of four fleet folds. On Ida, where the regret-robust allocation differed from the sample-average one, it moved units toward the boroughs the storm loaded and cost less than the sample-average design.

item.title: Online Covariance Estimation for Averaged Stochastic Gradient Descent on Riemannian Manifolds
item.description: We study online inference for averaged Riemannian stochastic gradient descent (RSGD) when the unknown parameter lies on a manifold. Although the averaged RSGD iterate is asymptotically normal, practical inference requires estimating the unknown covariance operator in its limiting distribution. Existing online batch-means methods cannot be applied directly because a general Riemannian manifold lacks an addition operation, and the tangent space containing the Riemannian gradient varies across iterations. Through vector transport, we construct overlapping and non-overlapping covariance estimators that adaptively combine information from successive batches while accounting for the changing tangent spaces. The proposed estimators are online, require neither Riemannian Hessian computations nor a prespecified terminal sample size, and attain the same convergence rates as their Euclidean counterparts (Zhu et al., 2023). Together with asymptotic normality, these estimators enable online statistical inference for RSGD on manifolds. We illustrate the proposed framework through a detailed study of streaming principal component analysis on Grassmann manifolds.

item.title: Affine-invariant Cubic Newton with Weak Learners
item.description: Modern gradient boosting algorithms are based on Newton's method, which excels empirically but lacks global convergence guarantees. While recent work on Gradient-Regularized Newton (GRN) boosting achieved a global $\mathcal{O}(1/γ^{12}k^2)$ rate, its analysis was not able to exploit the natural Hessian geometry and suffers from a heavy $γ^{12}$ dependence on a worst-case `weak gradient edge' $γ$. In this paper, we tackle these theoretical drawbacks by generalizing the Affine-Invariant Cubic Newton (AICN) scheme to convex optimization with weak learners. Our analysis is based on average cosine values $\overlineΘ_k$ along the optimization path and directional improvements $δ_k$ in the Hessian-induced norm. We show that the weak-AICN update reduces to a damped weak-Newton step with an explicit stepsize determined by $δ_k$. Under semi-strong self-concordance, we establish a global $\mathcal{O}(1/\overlineΘ_k^4 k^2)$ rate, significantly improving upon the weak-GRN bound. We further prove a local linear rate, global linear convergence for Hessian-dominated losses, cosine angle lower bounds, and present weak-AdaAICN, which adaptively tunes the cubic regularization. Finally, we demonstrate the broader applicability of this framework beyond gradient boosting by showing that Newton coordinate descent emerges naturally as a special case of optimization with weak learners.

item.title: Approximate Controllability of Neutral Integro-Differential Inclusions Associated with Hemivariational Inequalities in Banach Spaces with Uniformly Convex Dual
item.description: In this paper, we investigate the approximate controllability of neutral integro-differential inclusions driven by hemivariational inequalities with nonlocal inclusion conditions in a Banach space $\mathbb{V}$ whose dual $\mathbb{V}^*$ is uniformly convex, using resolvent operator theory. We first establish an equivalence between the original problem and an associated differential inclusion involving the Clarke subdifferential. Under suitable assumptions, we then prove the existence of mild solutions corresponding to admissible controls in $\mathrm{L}^2(I,\mathbb{U})$. A key contribution of this work lies in the analysis of the control construction in Banach spaces, where the duality mapping $\mathcal{J} = \partial\big(\tfrac{1}{2}\|\cdot\|_{\mathbb{V}}^2\big)$ is generally nonlinear, in contrast to the Hilbert space setting, while such nonlinearity has been viewed as a technical obstruction in earlier studies. Based on this framework, we prove approximate controllability of the original system by relating it to the controllability of the associated linearized inclusion and constructing appropriate controls involving the duality mapping. Finally, we present applications to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

item.title: Physics-Informed Graph-Based Safe RL with Constraint-Specific Critics for Community Battery Coordination in Distribution Network
item.description: High penetrations of distributed energy resources (DERs) and fast-varying electric vehicle (EV) charging intensify voltage and line-limit violations in distribution networks (DNs), making safe, low-cost operation increasingly challenging. This paper proposes a physics-informed safe deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework for coordinating community battery energy storage systems to mitigate constraint violations while minimizing operating cost. To represent nonlocal spatiotemporal interactions, we develop a dual-level physics-informed graph representation in which line impedance and capacity shape spatial information propagation, while power-balance, voltage-profile, and flow-reconstruction losses regularize the latent state toward control-relevant physical consistency. Building on this representation, we develop Lagrangian Dedicated-Critic PPO (LDCPPO), which implements constraint-specific value decomposition: independent reward and cost critics preserve heterogeneous voltage- and line-loading-related learning signals and combine their advantages only during the Lagrangian policy update. Case studies on DNs with high rooftop photovoltaic penetration and EV charging demonstrate that the proposed method reduces the key voltage-violation degree by up to 80.5% compared with the tested baselines, while also achieving the lowest voltage-violation count and line-overload degree with competitive operating cost.

item.title: On optimal stopping problems with full information and rank-dependent reward
item.description: In this paper we consider optimal stopping problems with full information and rank-dependent rewards. Our focus is on the following two problems: selecting one of the r best observations (Gusein-Zade's problem with full information) and minimizing the expected rank (Robbins' problem). In both settings we provide full characterization of the optimal stopping rules and corresponding optimal values. We also present numerical experiments in which the derived dynamic programming recursions are implemented, and approximations to optimal values are computed.

item.title: Multi-marginal optimal transport on sub-Riemannian manifolds
item.description: In this paper, we study multi-marginal optimal transport on ideal sub-Riemannian manifolds. We establish a sub-Riemannian barycentric balance condition and prove the existence of a solution to the Monge problem under an additional assumption. We also investigate the absolute continuity of Wasserstein barycenters. Our results extend and improve upon those of Pass, Pinamonti, and Vedovato (Methods Appl. Anal. 28 (2021), 61-76) on the Heisenberg group, answering two open questions raised in their work.

item.title: When Protection Hurts: A Cytokine Storm Theory of Supply Chain Overreaction
item.description: Supply chain resilience research has traditionally viewed defensive actions such as safety stock, backup suppliers, expedited transportation, and emergency sourcing as beneficial. However, disruptions such as the COVID-19 pandemic, the 2021 semiconductor shortage, and the Suez Canal blockage highlight how synchronized hoarding, duplicate ordering, and capacity reservation can amplify congestion and operational costs, sometimes worsening the original disruption. Motivated by this observation, we develop a decision-theoretic framework in which Protective Response Intensity (PRI) is an endogenous decision variable. We introduce Response-Induced Loss (RIL) to capture costs generated by defensive actions and characterize a unique optimal response that balances disruption mitigation against self-induced losses. We derive a closed-form critical response threshold beyond which RIL exceeds the original disruption intensity, a phenomenon termed a *Supply Chain Cytokine Storm*. We further propose the Cytokine Storm Index (CSI), measuring response-induced loss relative to the original disruption, and discuss its potential calibration using operational data. Extending the framework to interconnected supply networks, we derive a spectral stability condition distinguishing bounded decentralized responses from network-wide propagation. Numerical experiments show that optimal responses remain below the storm threshold, whereas proportional response heuristics can exceed it. Network responses converge or diverge according to the derived stability condition. Overall, our findings highlight that supply chain resilience depends not only on mitigating disruptions but also on keeping defensive responses proportionate to the shocks they are intended to address.

item.title: Convergence Analysis of Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient Descent under Relaxed Assumptions
item.description: We study convergence rates of Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient Descent (NAG) method for convex optimization in both deterministic and stochastic settings. We focus on a more general smoothness condition raised from several machine learning problems empirically and theoretically. We show the accelerated convergence rate of order $\mathcal{O}\left(1/T^2\right)$ in terms of the function value gap, given access to exact gradients of objective functions, matching the optimal rate for standard smooth convex optimization in \citep{nesterov1983method}. Under the relaxed affine-variance noise assumption for stochastic optimization, we establish the high-probability convergence rate of order $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\sqrt{\log\left(1/δ\right)/T}\right)$ and this rate could improve to $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\log\left(1/δ\right)/T^2\right)$ when the noise parameters are sufficiently small. Here, $T$ denotes the total number of iterations and $δ$ is the probability margin. Up to logarithm factors, our probabilistic convergence rate reaches the same order of the expected rate obtained in \citep{ghadimi2016accelerated} where the assumptions of bounded variance noise and Lipschitz smoothness are required. We additionally establish the convergence rates of the studied algorithms in the non-convex setting.

item.title: Optimal Control of the 2D Boussinesq Equations with Finite Codimension Constraints
item.description: We study an optimal control problem (OCP) governed by the two-dimensional (2D) Boussinesq equations, where the right-hand sides of the velocity and temperature equations are projected onto the corresponding tangent spaces of the manifolds $\mathcal{M}_1:=\{y\in\mathbb{H}:\|y\|_{\mathbb{H}}=1\}$ and $\mathcal{M}_2:=\{θ\in H:\|θ\|_H=1\}$, respectively. The resulting evolution is subject to finite-codimensional constraints, under which the state $(y,θ)$ remains on $\mathcal{M}:=\mathcal{M}_1\times\mathcal{M}_2$ throughout the time interval. A Faedo--Galerkin construction provides a unique, global, strong solution to the constrained Boussinesq system for external controls $\mathfrak{H}\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb{H})$, along with uniform energy bounds. In addition, we establish the existence of an optimal triplet $(y^*,θ^*,\mathfrak{H}^*)$ that minimizes the quadratic cost subject to the constrained Boussinesq system. Necessary conditions of the first order are obtained through a coupled state--adjoint--control system. The optimal state $(y^*,θ^*)$ remains on $\mathcal{M}$, while the optimal control lies in the tangent space: $\mathfrak{H}^*(t)\in T_{y^*(t)}\mathcal{M}_1$, for all $t\in[0,T]$. We also show that the map $\mathfrak{H}\mapsto(y_{\mathfrak{H}},θ_{\mathfrak{H}})$ in $(C([0,T];\mathbb{H})\cap L^2(0,T;\mathbb{V}))\times(C([0,T];H)\cap L^2(0,T;V))$ is Fréchet differentiable. The linearized state is the unique weak solution to the constrained linearized Boussinesq system and satisfies the necessary tangency condition. Hence, the well-posedness and first-order optimality conditions are established for the Boussinesq system under nonlinear manifold constraints.

item.title: A Cubic Underestimator for Deterministic Global Optimization
